paragraphs.heading: Same atoms, different shapes
paragraphs.text: Isomers are molecules or polyatomic ions with the same molecular formula, meaning the same count of atoms of each element, but with those atoms arranged differently in space. Isomerism is the name for the fact that isomers exist or can exist. The word goes back to Greek isos, equal, and meros, part. Sharing a formula does not mean sharing behaviour: isomers need not have similar chemical or physical properties.

paragraphs.heading: Two main kinds
paragraphs.text: In structural, or constitutional, isomerism, the bonds linking the atoms are different. In stereoisomerism, or spatial isomerism, the bonds are the same but the atoms sit in different relative positions. These relationships form a hierarchy. Two chemicals may be the same constitutional isomer and still, on closer analysis, be stereoisomers of each other. How deep to look depends on the field of study and on which properties matter.

paragraphs.heading: Three ways to build C₃H₈O
paragraphs.text: Structural isomers keep the same formula but join their atoms in different ways. Take C₃H₈O. Two of its isomers are propanols, alcohols on a chain of three carbons, which differ only in where the hydroxyl group (−OH) attaches: at the end of the chain in propan-1-ol, or at the middle carbon in propan-2-ol, also called isopropyl alcohol. These two are positional isomers, differing in where a feature sits on a parent molecule. The third isomer, methoxyethane, is an ether: its oxygen links to two carbons, and all eight hydrogens bond straight to carbons.

paragraphs.heading: Not every drawing is new
paragraphs.text: A new way of drawing a molecule is not always a new isomer. A so-called 3-propanol is just 1-propanol with its carbons numbered from the other end, and ethoxymethane is the same molecule as methoxyethane. Among another set of three-carbon isomers, there is only one with a triple bond, propyne, and only one cyclopropene. Any other placement of those bonds just draws the three carbons in a different order.

paragraphs.heading: Mirror images
paragraphs.text: Stereoisomers have the same atoms joined by bonds of the same type, but differ in where those atoms sit in space. They come in two broad types, enantiomers and diastereomers, and enantiomers have identical physical properties while diastereomers do not. Enantiomers are mirror images that no rotation or shift can make coincide, like a left hand and a right hand, and such shapes are called chiral. A classic case is bromochlorofluoromethane, CHFClBr: seen from the hydrogen atom, the route F to Cl to Br runs clockwise in one form and counterclockwise in the other.

paragraphs.heading: Why they stay apart
paragraphs.text: To turn one form of CHFClBr into the other, those four atoms would at some point have to lie flat in one plane. That would badly strain or break their bonds to the carbon. The energy barrier is so high that at room temperature there is practically no conversion, so the two count as different configurations. Chlorofluoromethane, CH₂ClF, is different: it is not chiral, because a half-turn about a suitable axis gives its mirror image.
